tāyana.notes: SN 2.8 calls Tāyana a godling and former religious founder. He recites his verses before the Buddha, who repeats them to the monks the next morning. SN 2.10 has his name in the chapter’s closing list.

udaya.notes: DPD’s ascetic is Bāvarī’s student in Snp 5.1, who questions the Buddha in Snp 5.14 and appears among the questioners in Snp 5.18. AN 3.33 also cites his questions in the compound udayapañhe. The candidate describes the brahmin who fills the Buddha’s bowl at his home in SN 7.12. Only Udaya himself declares refuge there. The neighboring SN 7.11 concerns Bhāradvāja the farmer.

udena.notes: SN 35.127 names the king visiting Piṇḍola. MN 94 names the monk speaking with Ghoṭamukha. AN 8.70, DN 16, DN 24, SN 51.10 and Ud 6.1 explicitly name the Udena shrine at Vesālī, which lacks a candidate. Ud 7.10 also names the king with Sāmāvatī, under the separate DPD spelling Utena. The page references extend to SN 35.125–126 and MN 93.

udumbarikā.notes: DN 25 names Udumbarikā through her monastery for wanderers. Her title of queen and her role in building it come from the commentary.

udāyī.notes: Udāyī 01 explicitly names Paṇḍita Udāyī and recounts his debate with Pañcakaṅga in MN 59 and SN 36.19. AN 1.225 names Kāḷudāyī as foremost in inspiring families. Thag 15.2 attributes the elephant verses to Udāyī Thera. DPD uses AN 6.43 for Kāḷudāyī, and DPPN records competing attributions for that performance of the same verses. DPPN also treats the identification in MN 66 as tentative. AN 5.166, AN 6.29, AN 9.34, AN 9.42 and MN 136 give too little to distinguish the monk. MN 77 and MN 79 address the wanderer Sakuludāyī by his shorter name. AN 6.30 and SN 35.237 have Udāyī only in their chapter summaries. In SN 35.133 the monk teaches the brahmin lady at her second meal invitation, where the entry says third. AN 4.39 concerns the brahmin Ujjaya, while AN 4.40 concerns Udāyī. Claude: MN 66 has no pick: the readings differ, and both call the link tentative.

ugga.notes: DPD’s minister example, AN 4.187, lists Ugga among King Eḷeyya’s men who honor Rāmaputta. AN 7.7 calls its speaker a chief minister and has him describe Migāra’s wealth. The hundred thousand gold coins belong to Migāra. Two grouped IDs each cover both householders. AN 1.253 names Ugga of Vesālī for his gifts, and AN 1.254 names Uggata of Hatthigāma for attending the Saṅgha. AN 6.120–139 names them on successive lines 1.6 and 1.7. A single preferred entry would misidentify one man in each group. The list of householders with six qualities is here, though the citation for Ugga 05 lands in AN 9.42–43.

uggatasarīra.notes: AN 7.47 names Uggatasarīra, describes his preparations for sacrifice, and ends with his release of the animals. The entry’s citation lands in AN 9.34, where Udāyī questions Sāriputta about extinguishment.

ujjaya.notes: Thag 1.47 explicitly attributes its verse to Ujjaya Thera. The entry cites Thag 1.67, attributed to Ekadhammasavanīya. The brahmin asks about sacrifice in AN 4.39 and welfare in AN 8.55. At AN 8.55:1.3 he says pavāsaṁ gantukāmā, wishing to travel abroad, where the entry reads upavāsa, a retreat. AN 4.38 and AN 8.54 are neighboring discourses. AN 4.40 and AN 8.60 have Ujjaya only in their chapter summaries.

ujjenī.notes: Snp 5.1 names Ujjenī on the students’ route, and Isidāsī names the town in Thig 15.1. The placed citations are indirect. DN 19 names Māhissatī as the Avantis’ capital, and MN 108 mentions King Pajjota. MN 107 shares the cited page.

ujjuhāna.notes: Thag 11.1:1.2 uses ujjuhānova in a monsoon simile. Sujato reads it as a bird. Both DPD and DPPN preserve the alternative hill interpretation, which the verse alone cannot establish.

ukkaṭṭhā.notes: DN 3 names Pokkharasāti’s town. AN 4.36 places it on the road to Setavyā. MN 49 gives the Subhaga Forest at Ukkaṭṭhā as the starting point of the visit to Baka. The parallel SN 6.4 starts at Jeta’s Grove in Sāvatthī. The page references also reach AN 4.35 and SN 6.3.

upaka.notes: Upaka 01 covers both DPD senses. MN 26 and MN 85 name the Ājīvaka on the road to Isipatana. The entry reverses the direction in its opening sentence. SN 1.50 and SN 2.24 name Upaka among the seven freed in Aviha. Ghaṭīkāra reports their liberation. The entry connects this Upaka with the Ājīvaka through his later life. AN 4.188 explicitly names Maṇḍikā’s son. Its page reference extends to AN 4.187 and AN 4.189.

upananda.notes: MN 108 calls Upananda senāpati. MN 116:6.23 gives twelve across the names Ānanda, Nanda and Upananda. The count of four Upanandas is more specific than the verse. The Sakyan monk has no candidate.
